newsitem.title: UK: Agenda in sight for Northern Irish peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Agenda in sight for Northern Irish peace talks.

text.p: Northern Ireland's peace talks appeared to be close to starting in earnest on Tuesday after key parties, spurred on by fresh Irish Republican Army violence, agreed on an outline agenda after four months of deadlock.

Delegates said a five-point agenda to get the faltering negotiations started had been approved on Monday by seven out of nine parties at the talks, which were launched in June but quickly ran into the sand.

Agreement would allow negotiators representing all of Northern Ireland's political groups except the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein, to begin the first real discussion on a lasting political settlement since the talks began.

Delegates said adoption of an agenda would reinforce a two- year truce by Protestant Loyalists which was threatened by an IRA bomb at Britain's Northern Ireland army headquarters in Lisburn last week.

It would enable politicians representing the Loyalists, who battled for 27 years to keep the province British, to take part in real negotiations towards a lasting political settlement, the delegates said.

The Progressive Unionist Party and the Ulster Democratic Party, small groups with links to outlawed Loyalist militia, both called for progress to be made at the talks last week when the IRA brought its campaign of violence back to the province.
They also appealed to Loyalist militia not to follow the IRA down the path of violence but to maintain their truce and let their political spokesmen negotiate a settlement.

The IRA bombing, the first in Northern Ireland for two years, killed one British soldier, injured 20 and raised fears that Loyalists would return to the random killings in the Catholic community from which the IRA draws support.
Adoption of an agenda would further isolate the IRA and Sinn Fein, which both seek to end British rule of Northern Ireland and reunite it under Dublin's rule.
Sinn Fein is excluded from the negotiations to punish the IRA for the ending of its 17-month truce in February with a campaign of bombings in Britain and Germany.

The Northern Ireland peace talks have been bogged down since they were launched by Britain and Ireland in June under the chairmanship of former U.S. Senator George Mitchell, President Bill Clinton's Ireland adviser.
Unionist parties, which want the province to stay British, suspected Mitchell of favouring their Irish nationalist rival, the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP).
They sought to rewrite the terms of his chairmanship and define the rules of procedure in moves which prevented any discussion at all of Northern Ireland's future until now.
